drop.http-fundamentals-sr1-02: weak_card: strawman. Nobody who has studied HTTP thinks a resource needs a new URI when its content changes. Dropping it leaves r1 at 9 cards (5T/4F).
drop.http-fundamentals-sr1-03: weak_card: restates the RFC definition of a proxy and is disputable for interception proxies. r1 stays at 9 cards.
drop.http-fundamentals-sr1-08: weak_card: close paraphrase of the RFC 9110 §5.1 sentence, and the hedged 'unless ... or' clause marks it true. Dropping it also removes the proxy-connection-field-handling giveaway of sr10-10.
drop.http-fundamentals-sr2-01: weak_card: 'incidental' and 'compatible' give away the answer, and the card is a near-truism. r2 stays at 10 cards (5T/5F).
drop.http-fundamentals-sr2-05: weak_card: strawman ('standardized filter') that leaves the real misconception about GET content untested. r2 stays balanced at 5T/5F.
drop.http-fundamentals-sr3-02: weak_card: strawman and name giveaway ('Continue' is not final). r3 stays at 9 cards (4T/5F).
drop.http-fundamentals-sr3-03: weak_card: near-truism, since '201 Created' plus Location gives the answer away. r3 stays at 9 cards.
drop.http-fundamentals-sr3-08: weak_card: definition card that restates the 409 Conflict reason phrase. r3 stays at 9 cards (4T/5F).
drop.http-fundamentals-sr4-01: weak_card: strawman. Nobody who has studied would call 301 temporary. r4 stays at 10 cards (5T/5F).
drop.http-fundamentals-sr4-12: weak_card: near-truism, since a 3xx arrives before any HTML exists. r4 stays at 5T/5F.
drop.http-fundamentals-sr5-05: weak_card: definition card that restates what proactive negotiation means and closely paraphrases RFC 9110 §12.1. r5 stays at 11 cards (5T/6F).
drop.http-fundamentals-sr6-01: weak_card: wording giveaway ('weak' and the W/ prefix). r6 stays at 10 cards (5T/5F).
drop.http-fundamentals-sr6-03: weak_card: wrong actor (the client, not an origin server, makes a request conditional), so the card is false for two reasons. r6 stays at 5T/5F.
drop.http-fundamentals-sr7-02: weak_card: strawman (caching a 1xx), and it overlaps sr3-02 on interim versus final. r7 stays at 11 cards (6T/5F).
drop.http-fundamentals-sr8-03: weak_card: name giveaway, since it restates the min-fresh directive name. Dropped. sr8-11 is rewritten instead so that r8 keeps 9 cards.
drop.http-fundamentals-sr8-07: weak_card: name giveaway, since 'proxy'-revalidate obviously excludes private caches. Dropped. sr8-11 is rewritten to keep r8 at 9 cards.
drop.http-fundamentals-sr8-10: weak_card: name giveaway and definition card for stale-if-error. Dropped. With sr8-11 rewritten, r8 ends at 9 cards (4T/5F).
drop.http-fundamentals-sr11-05: weak_card: name giveaway, since the status code sits in a field named :status. r11 stays at 10 cards (5T/5F).
drop.http-fundamentals-sr11-12: weak_card: 'as proof that' gives away the false answer, and the last-stream ID detail is implementer depth. r11 stays at 5T/5F.
drop.http-fundamentals-sr12-02: weak_card: the possessive 'QUIC's integrated TLS 1.3 handshake' presupposes the fact. Dropping it leaves r12 at 10 cards (4T/6F), which is at the limit but not worse.
drop.http-fundamentals-sr12-04: out_of_scope: QPACK decoder blocking on dynamic-table insert counts is HTTP-stack implementer depth, not the QPACK fact the section scopes. r12 ends at 4T/6F.
drop.http-fundamentals-sr13-04: weak_card: tests the lenient, guessable side of Content-Type safelisting (text/plain with charset) instead of strict parsing, and the explanation implies the charset helps. r13 stays at 11 cards (5T/6F).
drop.http-fundamentals-sr14-09: weak_card: says only that clone() does what its name says, the qualifiers 'unused, unlocked' give it away, and the 'two branches' claim is not on the cited page. r14 stays at 11 cards (5T/6F).

http-fundamentals-sr12-11.title: RFC 7838 §3.1: Caching Alt-Svc Header Field Values

http-fundamentals-sr12-12.title: RFC 7838 §3.1: Caching Alt-Svc Header Field Values

http-fundamentals-sr1-05.reason: ambiguous: an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 recipient rejects an uppercase field name as malformed, so the card must pin the version. RFC 9110 §5.1: "Field names are case-insensitive". (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr1-05.statement: In HTTP/1.1, a recipient treats the field names Content-Type and content-type as the same field.
http-fundamentals-sr1-05.explanation: RFC 9110 defines field names as case-insensitive, so an HTTP/1.1 recipient matches Content-Type whatever its capitalization.

http-fundamentals-sr1-11.reason: ambiguous: the old wording mixed up http/https with host case, and RFC 9110 allows simple string comparison. Reworded to what the RFC states, that equivalent URIs "can be assumed to identify the same resource" and "The scheme and host are case-insensitive". The answer changes to true because a false 'identify different resources' would add another 'different' false tell. r1 becomes 5T/4F. (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr1-11.statement: RFC 9110 lets a recipient assume http URIs whose hosts differ only in letter case identify the same resource.
http-fundamentals-sr1-11.explanation: Scheme and host are case-insensitive in http and https URIs, and URIs that are equivalent after normalization can be assumed to identify the same resource.

http-fundamentals-sr2-02.reason: tell: removes the false-leaning 'classifies X as' template and the word 'different'. The fact (idempotence ignores differing responses) and the answer (false) are unchanged. (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr2-02.statement: A DELETE whose repeat gets 404 after a first 204 counts as non-idempotent under RFC 9110.
http-fundamentals-sr2-02.explanation: DELETE stays idempotent even when a repeated request gets a different response, such as 404 after 204. Idempotence concerns the intended effect on the server, not identical status codes.
http-fundamentals-sr2-02.misconception: A method is idempotent only if repeating it returns the same status code.

http-fundamentals-sr3-06.reason: tell: after the r3 drops, true statements averaged 10 characters shorter than false ones. This lengthens the shortest true card without changing its fact (401 carries WWW-Authenticate) or its answer (true). r3 is now T 82.0 vs F 84.0. (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr3-06.statement: An origin server sending 401 Unauthorized includes a WWW-Authenticate field in that response.
http-fundamentals-sr3-06.explanation: A server generating 401 must include a WWW-Authenticate challenge applicable to the target resource.

http-fundamentals-sr5-01.reason: tell: removes the 'treats X as a different Y' template, the strongest false tell. The fact (media type tokens are case-insensitive, RFC 9110 §8.3.1) and the answer (false) are unchanged. (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr5-01.statement: A recipient matches media type names such as Text/HTML and text/html case-sensitively.
http-fundamentals-sr5-01.explanation: Media type names are case-insensitive: changing the case of the type or subtype leaves the media type unchanged.
http-fundamentals-sr5-01.misconception: Media type names are case-sensitive, so Text/HTML and text/html differ.

http-fundamentals-sr5-04.reason: tell: removes the 'treats X as an instruction to' sub-template and the word 'different'. The fact (Content-Location is metadata, not a redirect; RFC 9110 §8.7) and the answer (false) are unchanged. (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr5-04.statement: A user agent follows a response's Content-Location field by requesting that URI.
http-fundamentals-sr5-04.explanation: Content-Location identifies a resource corresponding to the enclosed representation. The field is metadata, rather than a redirect instruction.
http-fundamentals-sr5-04.misconception: Content-Location works like Location and makes the user agent fetch another URI.

http-fundamentals-sr5-08.reason: ambiguous: the card described what an origin server does (many really fall back to English). Reworded to what the request means. RFC 9110 §12.4.1: "a request that does not contain the field implies that the sender has no preference on that dimension". (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr5-08.statement: Under RFC 9110, a request that omits Accept-Language signals a preference for English.
http-fundamentals-sr5-08.explanation: RFC 9110 says a request lacking a content negotiation field, such as Accept-Language, implies that the sender has no preference on that dimension.
http-fundamentals-sr5-08.misconception: A request without Accept-Language means the client prefers English.

http-fundamentals-sr8-09.reason: ambiguous: the statement dropped the condition that must-understand accompanies no-store, and it paraphrased the RFC. RFC 9111 §5.2.2.3: "A response that contains the must-understand directive SHOULD also contain the no-store directive. When a cache that implements the must-understand directive receives a response that includes it, the cache SHOULD ignore the no-store directive if it understands and implements the status code's caching requirements." The verifier's version dropped 'implements must-understand' from the actor, so I restored it. (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr8-09.statement: A cache that implements `must-understand` and the status code's caching rules should ignore an accompanying `no-store`.
http-fundamentals-sr8-09.explanation: RFC 9111 has senders pair must-understand with no-store, so caches lacking that support store nothing, while a cache meeting both conditions should ignore no-store.

http-fundamentals-sr8-11.reason: weak_card, rewritten instead of dropped: dropping all four weak r8 cards (03, 07, 10, 11) would leave 8 cards. The old card tied immutable to Authorization, which the prompt forbids. The replacement tests the r8-scoped RFC 8246 limit. RFC 8246 §2: "The immutable extension only applies during the freshness lifetime of the stored response. Stale responses SHOULD be revalidated as they normally would be in the absence of the immutable extension." I avoided 'lets' and 'even after', both false-leaning tells. (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr8-11.statement: Under RFC 8246, a client honoring `immutable` skips revalidation once the stored response is stale.
http-fundamentals-sr8-11.explanation: RFC 8246 limits immutable to the stored response's freshness lifetime: once that response is stale, a client should revalidate it as it would without immutable.
http-fundamentals-sr8-11.misconception: immutable means a stored response never needs revalidation, even after it goes stale.

http-fundamentals-sr10-02.reason: ambiguous: the statement pinned the server version but not the request version, and an HTTP/1.0 request may omit Host. RFC 9112 §3.2: "A server MUST respond with a 400 (Bad Request) status code to any HTTP/1.1 request message that lacks a Host header field and to any request message that contains more than one Host header field line or a Host header field with an invalid field value." I also removed the vague 'target URI appears elsewhere' from the explanation. (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr10-02.statement: A server answers an HTTP/1.1 request that omits the Host field with 400 Bad Request.
http-fundamentals-sr10-02.explanation: RFC 9112 makes a server send 400 for any HTTP/1.1 request that lacks Host, and for any request with more than one Host field line or an invalid Host value.

http-fundamentals-sr12-09.reason: tell: removes the 'treats X as the new Y' template and the word 'new'. The fact (Alt-Svc leaves the origin unchanged) and the answer (false) are unchanged. The source also moves from rfc7838.txt to the HTML section anchor. RFC 7838 §2: "Alternative services do not replace or change the origin for any given resource". (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr12-09.statement: A client using Alt-Svc switches the resource's origin to the alternative service's host.
http-fundamentals-sr12-09.explanation: Alt-Svc changes the connection route while the URI's original scheme, host and port continue to identify the resource's origin.
http-fundamentals-sr12-09.misconception: Using an alternative service moves the resource to a new origin at the alternative's host.

http-fundamentals-sr13-06.reason: ambiguous: Firefox and Safari stringify a ReadableStream body and send no preflight, so the card is pinned to the Fetch Standard. Fetch (Last Updated 6 October 2026): "The use-CORS-preflight flag is set if ... a ReadableStream object is used in a request", and the Request constructor step: "If this's request's mode is neither "same-origin" nor "cors", then throw a TypeError. Set this's request's use-CORS-preflight flag." Set volatility to may_change (browser support). (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr13-06.statement: In the Fetch Standard, a cross-origin fetch() POST with a ReadableStream body goes through CORS preflight.
http-fundamentals-sr13-06.explanation: A ReadableStream request body sets the request's use-CORS-preflight flag, so a cross-origin request is preflighted even with a safelisted method and headers.

http-fundamentals-sr13-11.reason: wrong_answer: as worded ('a browser can'), the statement is true in practice. MDN BCD http.headers.Access-Control-Allow-Headers.authorization_not_covered_by_wildcard, which I checked myself, lists Chrome, Edge and Safari as version_added false, and Firefox 115 only behind a preference. The replacement is pinned to the spec and confirmed. Fetch: "A CORS non-wildcard request-header name is a header name that is a byte-case-insensitive match for `Authorization`", and CORS-preflight fetch: "If one of request's header list's names is a CORS non-wildcard request-header name and is not a byte-case-insensitive match for an item in headerNames, then return a network error." I avoided 'lets', a false tell. Set appliesTo to Fetch Standard and volatility to may_change. (final: keep)
http-fundamentals-sr13-11.statement: In the Fetch Standard, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *` covers the Authorization request header.
http-fundamentals-sr13-11.explanation: The Fetch Standard makes Authorization a CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so a preflight passes only when Access-Control-Allow-Headers names it explicitly.
http-fundamentals-sr13-11.misconception: A * in Access-Control-Allow-Headers covers every request header, Authorization included.
